en: Sutta Nipāta 4.9 Māgaṇḍiyasutta “Having seen craving, aversion, and passion, ...”
There was not even a desire for sexual union;
how could one wish even to touch with the feet this thing filled with urine and excrement?
“If you do not desire such a jewel as this—
a woman sought after by many lords of men—
then what is the life of one who holds to dogmatic views or observes mere rules and vows?”
“And what kind of rebirth do you say there is?
“He does not think, ‘I say this,’ Māgaṇḍiya,” said the Blessed One.
Having discerned among the teachings what was well-grasped,
and seeing while not adhering to views,
I beheld the inner peace within myself.
“Those various speculative views that have been formulated—
these, O Sage, you have spoken of without grasping,” said Māgandiya.
"How is this matter of 'inner peace' proclaimed by the wise?
"Not by view, not by hearing, nor by knowledge."
(Māgaṇḍiya, said the Blessed One:
"One does not speak of purity through mere rules and observances;
nor through lack of wrong views, lack of learning, or lack of knowledge."
“Neither by lack of virtue nor by non-austerity is one [defiled];
having relinquished these and being without grasping,
the peaceful one, independent, should not yearn for existence.”
“If, indeed, it is not by view, nor by hearing, nor by knowledge— so said Māgandiya—
that one speaks of purity even through rules and observances;”
Through lack of vision, lack of hearing, and lack of knowledge,
through lack of virtue and lack of restraint— one does not [attain] by that means.
I consider such a doctrine to be merely deluded.
“Some declare purification through views.
“Relying on what has been seen,
Māgaṇḍiya,” the Blessed One said, “when one is questioned further...”
You have fallen into confusion regarding what has been grasped;
you did not perceive even the slightest sign from this [teaching],
and therefore you hold me in contempt because of your delusion.
Whether superior or inferior,
he who conceives such notions would dispute with him;
but one who is unshakable regarding these three states—
When there is only distinction, that does not exist for him.
What could that brahmin say regarding "truth," or with whom could he dispute regarding "falsehood"?
In whom there is neither even nor uneven,
with whom would he engage in dispute?
Having abandoned his home, wandering without a fixed abode—
The sage who forms no intimacies in the village,
free from sensual desires and seeking nothing for himself—
how could he engage in dispute with people?
One who wanders alone in the world should not speak while grasping at those things,
like a noble elephant [does not grasp] a lotus from the mud or one from the thorny water.
Unstained by water or mud,
even so the sage who speaks of peace and is free from greed is unstained by sensual pleasures and the world.
The one who has realized the Vedas is not led by views nor by wisdom;
he does not pride himself, for he is not made of that.
He is not to be led by action, nor even by learning.
He is not led into household dwellings.
For one who is detached from perceptions, there are no fetters;
for one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions.
“Those who have grasped at perception and views wander about in the world, clashing with one another.
Thus ends the ninth discourse, the *Māgaṇḍiya Sutta*.
